title: The Name that remains
hook: kings and their enemies pass; the ninth Guru names what stays

segments.voice: Yesterday, the world as dream: a show, a bubble on water. Your line was wake up gently.

Everyone in this photograph is gone now. It came out of a box in a closet: a wedding, maybe, or a family on a porch. The porch is gone. The clothes, the car, the town as it looked. On the back, in faded pencil, somebody wrote down who they were. Of everything in that picture, the writing has outlasted the people. Yesterday the ninth Guru called the world a dream. Today, near the very end of the Guru Granth Sahib, he names what doesn't drain away when you wake.
screen: `AN OLD PHOTOGRAPH IN A BOX.` → `EVERYONE IN IT IS GONE.` → `WHAT DOESN'T DRAIN AWAY?`

segments.voice: Two saloks, side by side, paraphrased. The first: Ram has gone, and Ravan has gone, though he had a great family; nothing is fixed, says Nanak, the world is like a dream. Ram and Ravan, the hero and the enemy of the Ramayana, a story Hindus hold sacred. Even the kings of that story, on both sides, passed from the earth. Then the turn. The second salok: the Name has remained; the holy ones have remained; the Guru, the Lord of the world, has remained. And a question: says Nanak, who in this world has truly repeated the Guru's mantra? So here's what stays. Not palaces, families or kingdoms. The Name, which Sikhs understand as the presence of God, remembered and repeated. The holy ones, the company of people who live that remembering. And the Guru, the Lord, the source of it all. The pencil on the photograph lasts a while, then fades too. The Name in this salok isn't writing on paper. It's what a life is pointed toward. When Sikhs remember the Name, saying Waheguru, singing the hymns, keeping it under the breath through a working day, they're touching the one thing the Guru says isn't part of the dream. That closing question is honest, not proud. The Guru doesn't claim everyone remembers; he asks who has. Some readers hear a quiet invitation in it: be one who does, once more today. If a loss is heavy on you right now, you don't have to carry it alone: in the US, call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.
screen: `RAM AND RAVAN HAVE GONE.` · `THE NAME, THE HOLY, THE GURU REMAIN.` · `NOT WRITING ON PAPER.` · `WHO HAS REPEATED THE MANTRA?` · then, large: `IT REMAINS.`

segments.voice: Let the passing things of your day drift by, the inbox, the dishes, the news, like pictures in a closet box. Then come back to one thing that stays: if you pray, repeat Waheguru quietly once on each breath; if not, choose one word for what lasts for you and return to it whenever the mind wanders. Once more, and once more.
The Name that remains. When kings, families and kingdoms pass, the ninth Guru's salok says the Name, the holy ones and the Guru remain. Today's word.
Your line: it remains. Whatever passes, the Name still stays. Back tomorrow, same hill.

howItsDone: These saloks of Guru Tegh Bahadur are read near the close of a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs practice naam simran, remembering the Name, by repeating Waheguru and singing gurbani.

chat.says: Everything passes, the Guru says. So what's left when it's all gone?

Nothing at all; the salok says even the Name fades in the end.
